title: Determinant
body:
The **determinant** of a square [[Matrix]] is a single number $\det A$ (also written $|A|$)
that answers one question: **by how much does this matrix scale volume, and does it flip
orientation?**

Lead with that. Cofactor expansion is how you compute it and it explains nothing; the
geometric reading is what makes every property in this note obvious.

## The geometric reading

Take the columns of $A$ as vectors. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ they span a parallelogram; in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, a parallelepiped. **$|\det A|$ is that area or volume**, and the sign records
whether the [[Linear Transformation]] preserved orientation (positive) or mirrored it
(negative).

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = 6
$$

which is exactly the area of the $3 \times 2$ rectangle the columns make. Read as a
transformation, this matrix stretches the plane by $3$ horizontally and $2$ vertically, so every
region it touches comes out $6$ times bigger.

Everything else follows:

- **$\det A = 0$ means the columns are flat.** They collapsed into a lower dimension, so the
  volume is zero, so the transformation destroyed information and cannot be undone. That is
  exactly why $\det A = 0$ is the same statement as "$A$ has no [[Matrix Inverse]]" and as
  "the columns are [[Linear Dependence|linearly dependent]]".
- **$\det(AB) = \det A \det B$.** Scale by one factor, then the other. This is the least
  obvious algebraic property in the chapter and the most obvious geometric one.
- **$\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det A$.** Undoing a scaling by $k$ scales by $1/k$.
- **$\det(A^T) = \det A$.** The row parallelepiped and the column one have the same volume.

## Computing it

**$2 \times 2$**, which you should know by reflex:

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc
$$

**$3 \times 3$ and up: cofactor expansion.** Pick any row or column, and for each entry
multiply it by the determinant of the matrix left when you delete its row and column (the
**minor** $M_{ij}$), with an alternating sign:

$$
\det A = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{i+j} a_{ij} M_{ij}
$$

The $(-1)^{i+j}$ signs form a checkerboard starting with $+$ in the top left:

```
+ - +
- + -
+ - +
```

Worked, expanding along the first row:

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix}
= 1(50 - 48) - 2(40 - 42) + 3(32 - 35) = 2 + 4 - 9 = -3
$$

**Expand along whichever row or column has the most zeros.** Any choice gives the same answer,
so this is free.

**Best method for anything larger: row reduce.** A triangular matrix has determinant equal to
the product of its diagonal, so run [[Gaussian Elimination]] and multiply the pivots, tracking
what the row operations did:

| Row operation | Effect on $\det$ |
|---|---|
| swap two rows | multiplies by $-1$ |
| scale a row by $c$ | multiplies by $c$ |
| add a multiple of a row to another | **no change** |

That third row is the useful one, and the geometric reading explains it: shearing a
parallelogram sideways slides the top along without changing base or height.

## Cost, and why it matters

Cofactor expansion recurses into $n$ subproblems of size $n-1$, giving $O(n!)$. Row reduction is
$O(n^3)$. For $n = 20$ that is the difference between $2 \times 10^{18}$ operations and about
$8000$: unusable versus instant. This is one of the cleanest illustrations in the degree of what
[[Time Complexity]] is actually for, and it belongs beside the sorting bounds in
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]].

## Where it shows up

- **Invertibility**: $\det A \neq 0$ is the test. See the equivalence table in
  [[Matrix Inverse]].
- **[[Cramer's Rule]]**: solves a system as a ratio of determinants.
- **The characteristic equation** $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$, which is how you find
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]. This is the determinant's most important job in the course,
  and it works because you are asking which $\lambda$ makes $A - \lambda I$ collapse.
- **Change of variables in integration**: the Jacobian determinant is the local volume
  scaling factor, which is why $dx\,dy$ becomes $r\,dr\,d\theta$ in polar coordinates. Taken
  properly in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] under [[Multiple Integration]].

Shortcuts worth having: a triangular matrix's determinant is the product of the diagonal, and a
matrix with a zero row, a zero column, or two identical rows has determinant $0$.

- [[Linear Transformation]] is what it measures
